correctness.rationale: Integrating the unscaled beta density and counting the k−1 outward edges gives the mean in the finding. At x=1/k the derivative of (1−x)F_b(x)/x has the sign of q_b(x)−1, where q_b'(x)=b(b+1)x(1−x)^(b−1)[1−(b+2)x]. The rise above 1 and fall to 0 prove strict unimodality for every real b>0, including b<1. The high-degree limit is 0 and strict monotonicity on either side gives the stated integer consequences. At k=2 the mean is below 1; at k=3 it increases with b and is 262/243 at b=4. Rounding a strict continuous upper crossing gives ceil(c_b)−1, also at integer crossings. The rescaled stationary equation has a unique positive crossing bounded away from zero and infinity, and converges uniformly on the resulting compact interval; floor/ceiling of the peak give the integer maximizing scale and the maximum coefficient. For k=b²/2+tb a Taylor expansion of the density integrand, uniform for bounded t, gives coefficients −2t−1/3 and 4t²+(10/3)t−1 at orders 1/b and 1/b². Setting t=−1/6+u/b and bracketing by bounded u on the descending branch gives the residual coefficient −2u−13/9 and hence the continuous constant −13/18 with O(1/b) remainder. Independent high-precision bisection at noninteger b agrees; it is not the proof.
residual_risks: The proof is for local vulnerable-branching supercriticality, not global cascade probability, size or a finite-graph law. No formal or expert certification is claimed.

value.rationale: Knowing where vulnerable propagation is strongest is a different practical and mathematical question from knowing how far connectivity can rise before it fails. The theorem separates their scales by a growing order of magnitude and gives both a precise finite connectivity window and a sharp descending boundary, for a natural threshold family. This is more than a substitution in the known branching formula.
residual_risks: The conclusions depend on the unscaled varying-mean family and do not imply corresponding laws under fixed-mean rescaling or degree heterogeneity.
